The papers that made the modern mind.

Eighteen waves of works — spanning twenty-six centuries. Wave 18 — the deepest classical and contemplative. Aristotle's Metaphysics 350 BC (being is said in many ways), Euclid's Elements 300 BC (geometry is a deductive system), Archimedes 250 BC (mathematics is the key to nature), Ptolemy's Almagest 150 AD (the cosmos is mathematical), Laozi's Tao Te Ching 500 BC (the Tao that cannot be spoken), Zhuangzi 300 BC (the equality of things), the Upanishads 800 BC (tat tvam asi), the Bhagavad Gita 200 BC (you have the right to action alone), the Dhammapada 100 BC (mind is the forerunner), Shankara 800 AD (atman is Brahman), the Mumonkan 1228 (Mu), Capra 1975 (the Tao of Physics), Faraday 1831 (electromagnetic induction), Helmholtz 1847 (conservation of force), Helmholtz 1867 (unconscious inference), Helmholtz 1882 (music is physics), Babbage 1822 (the analytical engine), Lovelace 1843 (the first algorithm), Engelbart 1968 (the Mother of All Demos), de Tocqueville 1835 (the tyranny of the majority), Pareto 1916 (the circulation of elites), Heidegger 1935 (art is truth happening), Heidegger 1937 (being is event), Adorno 1970 (the truth content of art), Ibn Khaldun 1377 (the cycle of civilization), Bush 1945 (memex), McLuhan 1964 (the medium is the message). Each entry is given in four voices: the version a curious child can hold, the counter-intuitive flash that connects to today, the version a sharp A-level student deserves, and the version a doctoral examiner would accept.

About the four layers

Every paper carries four layers, written so that the same idea reaches you at whatever altitude you're standing on today.

Wave 1 (31): foundational papers in AI-adjacent fields. Wave 2 (62): broader categories — ancient studies, theology, anthropology, architecture, music, film, astronomy, geology, chemistry, medicine. Wave 3 (51): truly universal ideas — one sentence unlocks thousands. Wave 4 (48): AI and neural networks in depth. Wave 5 (25): the originals — forgotten founders, pre-prints, original equations. Wave 6 (22): hidden foundations — pre-modern originals. Wave 7 (25): forgotten first authors — papers that already had the answer decades before the field got credit (Cauchy, de Moivre, Laplace, Linnainmaa, Ivakhnenko). Wave 8 (25): the untranslated originals — Soviet preprints, Italian doctoral theses, UK Ministry reports, French posthumous books (Lyapunov 1892, Monge 1781, Kotelnikov 1933, Manin 1980, Wiesner 1983). Wave 9 (25): the genuinely unread — unpublished memos, Spanish ring networks, French cybernetics, Soviet probability in Italian journals (Pitts 1942, Lorente de Nó 1938, Hayek 1952, Khachiyan 1979, Glivenko 1933). Wave 10 (25): the universal sentences — papers where one sentence unlocks thousands of things (Carnot 1824, Gauss 1827, Galois 1832, Hardy 1908, Bell 1964, Wolpert 1996). Wave 11 (25): number theory & primes — the deepest laws about the integers (Fermat 1640, Euler 1740, Riemann 1859, Hadamard 1896, Selberg 1949, Green-Tao 2008, AKS 2002). Wave 12 (24): the most universal principles — meta-laws that unlock thousands of things (Aristotle, Leibniz, Maupertuis, Hume, Kant, Comte, Mill, Peirce, Frege, Russell, Wittgenstein, Popper, Cox, Jaynes, Spencer-Brown, Anderson, Bak, Prigogine). Wave 13 (23): the deepest meta-principles — self-reference, fixed-points, conservation of information, autopoiesis, strange loops. Wave 14 (62): the deepest unifiers — variational, Noether, information-as-substrate, hierarchy, why anything exists, qualia, HoTT. Wave 15 (30): the foundations of everything — foundational papers across every domain. Wave 16 (79): the deepest foundations — the primary sources of every tradition. Mathematics (Euler, Gauss, Riemann, Hilbert, Noether, Freyd, Kan, Cartan-Eilenberg, Brown). Physics (Newton, Maxwell, Einstein 1905/1915, Schrödinger, Schwinger, Weinberg, Gross-Wilczek, Higgs). Biology (Schleiden, Morgan, Burnet, Avery-Macleod-McCarty, Meselson-Stahl, Jacob-Monod). CS (Boole, Frege, Russell-Whitehead, Knuth, Chaitin, Hoare). Psychology (Wundt, Fechner, James, Wertheimer). Sociology (Hobbes, Locke, Rousseau, Tönnies, Simmel, Weber, Goffman). Anthropology (Herodotus, Morgan, Boas, Malinowski). Linguistics (Pāṇini, Sapir). Music (Boethius, Monteverdi, Glareanus). Architecture (Wren, Wright). Philosophy (Heraclitus, Descartes, Locke, Berkeley, Kant 1788, Kierkegaard, Nietzsche, Heidegger 1953, Spinoza, Hegel, Schopenhauer, Wittgenstein 1953). Economics (Malthus, Schumpeter, Hayek, Simon, Coase). Mystical/Contemplative (Dōgen, Pseudo-Dionysius). Default: Wave 16.

  • Elementary — one vivid sentence, no jargon, true to the heart of the idea.
  • ⚡ Aha — the counter-intuitive flash that connects the paper to your life today.
  • Abitur — what a sharp A-level / Abitur student should walk away with after a thoughtful reading.
  • PhD — the precise claim, the technical apparatus, and the non-obvious consequence.

Curated to complement (not duplicate) the asanAI course. PDFs link to public archives where possible; some links point to publisher pages where the original is paywalled.
